content: UN numbers, also referred to as UN IDs, are four-digit numerical codes that are used to identify hazardous substances and articles, such as explosives, flammable liquids, and toxic substances, within the context of international transportation. For example, flammable liquids that are not otherwise specified are assigned the UN number 1993. A chemical in its solid state may be assigned a different UN number than its liquid state if their hazardous properties differ significantly. Similarly, substances with varying levels of purity or differing concentrations in solution may also be assigned distinct UN numbers. The range of UN numbers extends from UN 0001 to approximately UN 3500. These numbers are assigned by the United Nations Committee of Experts on the Transport of Dangerous Goods. The assignments are published as part of the Recommendations on the Transport of Dangerous Goods, commonly referred to as the Orange Book. These recommendations are adopted by regulatory organizations responsible for overseeing different modes of transportation. In North America, NA numbers, also known as DOT numbers, are issued by the United States Department of Transportation. These numbers are identical to UN numbers, except in cases where certain substances that do not have a UN number are assigned an NA number. These additional NA numbers fall within the range of NA 8000 to NA 9999. Each UN number is associated with a hazard identifier, which encodes the general hazard class and subdivision of the substance. In the case of explosives, the hazard identifier also includes the compatibility group. If a substance poses multiple hazards, subsidiary risk identifiers may also be specified. However, it is not possible to deduce the hazard class or classes of a substance solely from its UN number; this information must be looked up in a reference source.
